questions.knowledge_point: Finding the First Terms of the Taylor Series of a Function About a Point
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $a=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ f\,(-\frac{\pi }{2}) & =sin\,(-\frac{\pi }{2})=-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}\,(-\frac{\pi }{2}) & =cos\,(-\frac{\pi }{2})=0 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}\,(-\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-sin\,(-\frac{\pi }{2})=1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{‴}\,(-\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-cos\,(-\frac{\pi }{2})=0 \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{(4)}\,(-\frac{\pi }{2}) & =sin\,(-\frac{\pi }{2})=-1. \\ \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-1+0\,(x+\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{1}{2!}\,{(x+\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+\frac{0}{3!}\,{(x+\frac{\pi }{2})}^{3}+\frac{(-1)}{4!}\,{(x+\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}+⋯ \\  & =-1+\frac{1}{2}\,{(x+\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}-\frac{1}{24}\,{(x+\frac{\pi }{2})}^{4}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the First Terms of the Taylor Series of a Function About a Point
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's theorem in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)$ and $a=e.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) \\ f(e) & =e\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)=e \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1 \\ {f}^{′}(e) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡e+1=2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{1}{x} \\ {f}^{″}(e) & =\frac{1}{e} \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{‴}(e) & =-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) & =e+(2)(x-e)+\frac{(\frac{1}{e})}{2!}(x-e)^{2}-\frac{(\frac{1}{{e}^{2}})}{3!}(x-e)^{3}⋯ \\  & =e+2(x-e)+\frac{1}{2e}(x-e)^{2}⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of $\operatorname{cos}⁡2x$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's theorem in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x$ and $a=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)\,\,\,\, & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=-2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ {f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=0 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\ {f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x & =0+(-2)(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{(0)}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+\frac{(8)}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3}+⋯ \\  & =-2(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{4}{3}{(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{3}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the First Terms of the Taylor Series of a Function About a Point
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's theorem in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+x$ and $a=1.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+x \\ f(1) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1=1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x}+1 \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =1+1=2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(1) & =-1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{2}{{x}^{3}} \\ {f}^{‴}(1) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+x & =1+2(x-1)+\frac{-1}{2!}(x-1)^{2}+\frac{2}{3!}(x-1)^{3}⋯ \\  & =1+2(x-1)-\frac{1}{2}(x-1)^{2}+\frac{1}{3}(x-1)^{3}⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Approximating the Value of a Function at a  Point Using Its Taylor Series
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $a=1.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt{x}={x}^{1/2} \\ f(1) & ={1}^{1/2}=1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{2}){x}^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{″}(1) & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x} & =1+\frac{1}{2}(x-1)+\frac{(-1/4)}{2!}(x-1)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =1+\frac{1}{2}(x-1)-\frac{1}{8}(x-1)^{2}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=1.2$ into the above to approximate $\sqrt{1.2}.$ Since

$$
1.2-1=\frac{1}{5},
$$

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1.2} & ≈1+\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{5})-\frac{1}{8}{(\frac{1}{5})}^{2} \\  & =1+\frac{1}{10}-\frac{1}{200} \\  & =\frac{219}{200}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion for $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ about $x=\pi $ to approximate the value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡3.$ Give your answer to $5$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=\pi .$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ f(\pi ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi =0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\pi ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi =0 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{‴}(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =(0)+(-1)(x-\pi )+\frac{(0)}{2!}(x-\pi )^{2}+\frac{(1)}{3!}(x-\pi )^{3}+⋯ \\  & =-(x-\pi )+\frac{1}{6}(x-\pi )^{3}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=3$ into the above to approximate $\operatorname{sin}⁡3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡3 & ≈-(3-\pi )+\frac{1}{6}(3-\pi )^{3} \\  & =0.141\,12,\end{aligned}
$$

to five decimal places.

questions.problem: Use the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of  $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ about $x=\pi $ to approximate the value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi +1).$ Give your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=\pi .$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ f(\pi ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi =0 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(\pi ) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{‴}(\pi ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi =0 \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{(4)}(\pi ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =-1+\frac{1}{2!}(x-\pi )^{2}-\frac{1}{4!}(x-\pi )^{4}+⋯ \\  & =-1+\frac{1}{2}(x-\pi )^{2}-\frac{1}{24}(x-\pi )^{4}+⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=\pi +1$ into the above to approximate $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi +1).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi +1) & ≈-1+\frac{1}{2}(\pi +1-\pi )^{2}-\frac{1}{24}(\pi +1-\pi )^{4} \\  & =-1+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{24} \\  & =-0.542,\end{aligned}
$$

to $3$ decimal places.

questions.problem: Use the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of ${x}^{1/3}$ about $x=8$ to approximate the value of ${7}^{1/3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=8.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{1/3} \\ f(8) & ={8}^{1/3}=2 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{-2/3} \\ {f}^{′}(8) & =\frac{1}{3}(8)^{-2/3}=\frac{1}{3\cdot 4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{1/3} & =2+\frac{1}{3\cdot 4}(x-8)+⋯ \\  & =2+\frac{x-8}{12}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=7$ into the above to approximate ${7}^{1/3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{7}^{1/3} & ≈2+\frac{7-8}{12} \\  & =2-\frac{1}{12} \\  & =\frac{23}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion for $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ about $x=\pi $ to approximate the value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡4.$ Give your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=\pi .$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ f(\pi ) & =-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\pi ) & =0 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(\pi ) & =1 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{‴}(\pi ) & =0 \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{(4)}(\pi ) & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =-1+(0)(x-\pi )+\frac{(1)}{2!}(x-\pi )^{2}+\frac{(0)}{3!}(x-\pi )^{3}+\frac{(-1)}{4!}(x-\pi )^{4}⋯ \\  & =-1+\frac{1}{2!}(x-\pi )^{2}-\frac{1}{4!}(x-\pi )^{4}⋯\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=4$ into the above to approximate $\operatorname{cos}⁡4.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡4 & ≈-1+\frac{1}{2!}(4-\pi )^{2}-\frac{1}{4!}(4-\pi )^{4} \\  & =-1+\frac{1}{2}(4-\pi )^{2}-\frac{1}{24}(4-\pi )^{4} \\  & =-0.654\,,\end{aligned}
$$

to three decimal places.

canonical_examples.problem: Use the first three terms of the Taylor expansion for $f(x) = \sqrt x$ about $x=9$ to approximate the value of $\sqrt{9.1}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use Taylor's theorem in the form

$$
f(x)	= f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \frac{f''(a)}{2!}(x-a)^2 +\cdots,
$$

with $a=9.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{1/2} \\ f(9) & =3 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\ {f}^{′}(9) & =\frac{1}{6} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{″}(9) & =-\frac{1}{108}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x} & =3+\frac{1}{6}(x-9)+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{108})(x-9)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =3+\frac{1}{6}(x-9)-\frac{1}{216}(x-9)^{2}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x = 9.1$ into the above to approximate $\sqrt{9.1}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{9.1} & ≈3+\frac{1}{6}(9.1-9)-\frac{1}{216}(9.1-9)^{2} \\  & ≈3+\frac{1}{6}(0.1)-\frac{1}{216}(0.1)^{2} \\  & =3.016\,620,\end{aligned}
$$

to six decimal places. 

**Note:** The exact value of $\sqrt{9.1}$ is $3.016\,621$ to six decimal places. So, our approximation is very good!
